q: Ferranti effect in a transmission line means:
options: Corona loss rises in wet weather
Receiving-end voltage exceeds sending-end voltage at light or no load
Sending-end voltage exceeds receiving-end voltage at full load
explanation: Line shunt capacitance draws a leading charging current; flowing through the series inductance it raises receiving-end voltage on long, lightly loaded lines.
why: That is normal regulation under load, not Ferranti.
That is not the Ferranti effect.

q: Ferranti effect is mainly due to the line’s:
explanation: Capacitive charging current through series inductive reactance produces a voltage rise. Shunt reactors are used to control it.
why: Skin effect only raises AC resistance.
Resistance causes a drop, not a rise.

q: Ferranti effect is most pronounced on:
options: Long EHV lines at no load
explanation: Charging current grows with line length and voltage; at no load nothing offsets it. DC lines have no charging current in steady state.
why: Short lines have negligible capacitance and full load masks it.
No steady charging current on DC.

q: Shunt reactors are installed at the receiving end of long EHV lines to:
options: Improve power factor of industrial loads
Absorb reactive power and limit voltage rise at light load
explanation: They compensate line charging (capacitive) VArs, limiting the Ferranti rise.
why: Skin effect is a conductor property.
Industrial pf correction uses shunt capacitors.

q: Corona is the:
options: Ionisation of air around a conductor when the surface field exceeds the air’s breakdown strength
Heating of a conductor due to load current
Sag of a line in hot weather
explanation: Above the critical disruptive voltage (≈30 kV/cm peak, 21.1 kV/cm rms in normal air) air near the surface ionises, giving a violet glow, hissing, ozone and power loss.

q: Corona loss on a line can be reduced by:
options: Increasing conductor diameter or using bundled conductors
explanation: Larger effective diameter lowers the surface electric field. Bundled conductors and hollow/ACSR conductors are used on EHV lines.

q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of corona?
options: It reduces the steepness of travelling surge waves
explanation: The extra (virtual) capacitance from the corona envelope attenuates and flattens the front of lightning/switching surges.

q: Corona effect is greater in:
explanation: Moisture and drops on the surface lower the critical disruptive voltage (lower irregularity and air density factors).
why: Dry air raises the breakdown threshold.
Fair weather gives the least corona.

q: Skin effect means:
options: DC current flows on the surface
Alternating current tends to concentrate near the surface of the conductor
Current is uniform over the cross-section at all frequencies
explanation: Inner filaments link more flux and have higher reactance, so AC crowds to the outer layer, raising effective resistance.

q: Skin effect increases with:
options: Increase in frequency and conductor diameter
explanation: Skin depth δ = √(ρ/(πfμ)); higher f and larger diameter (or μ) increase the effect.
why: There is no skin effect on DC.

q: Hollow or ACSR conductors are used in EHV lines mainly to:
explanation: A larger diameter for the same material reduces surface stress (corona); since AC flows mainly in the outer part anyway, inner material is wasted — skin effect.
why: Steel core in ACSR increases strength.

q: In an ACSR conductor, the steel core provides:
explanation: Aluminium strands carry current; the galvanised steel core carries the mechanical load allowing long spans.
why: Bare overhead conductors are not insulated.

q: Surge impedance of a lossless transmission line is given by:
explanation: Z_{c} = √(L/C); typically ≈ 400 Ω for single-circuit overhead lines and 40–60 Ω for cables.
why: That has units of time per length; related to propagation delay.

q: Typical surge impedance of an overhead transmission line is about:
explanation: Overhead lines: 300–500 Ω (≈400 Ω); bundling reduces it. Underground cables: 30–60 Ω.

q: Surge impedance loading of a 220 kV line with surge impedance 400 Ω is about:
When a line is loaded exactly at its surge impedance loading:
options: Reactive power generated by line capacitance equals reactive power absorbed by its inductance
explanation: At SIL, ½CV^{2} = ½LI^{2} per unit length: the line is reactively self-compensated and the voltage profile is flat.
why: Load at SIL is resistive (Z_{c}), unity pf.

q: Pin-type insulators are generally used up to:
explanation: Beyond about 33 kV pin insulators become too large and costly; suspension (disc) strings are used for higher voltages.
why: Long suspension strings are used at 500 kV.
They are used well above 3.3 kV.
Suspension insulators are used at 132 kV.

q: Strain insulators are used:
options: At dead ends, sharp corners and river crossings
explanation: They take the full mechanical tension of the conductor where the line terminates or changes direction sharply.
why: Shackle insulators are typical for LV.
Suspension strings are used on straight runs.

q: In a string of suspension insulators, the voltage across the disc nearest to the line conductor is:
explanation: Shunt (disc-to-tower) capacitance makes the bottom disc carry the most charging current, so it has the highest voltage. Guard (grading) rings and longer cross-arms improve distribution.
why: The disc nearest the cross-arm has the least voltage.
Only if shunt capacitance were zero.

q: A 4-disc string has 66 kV across it, and the disc nearest the conductor has 20 kV. String efficiency is:
why: Ratio of one disc’s voltage to the string voltage is not efficiency.

q: String efficiency can be improved by:
explanation: A grading ring adds line-to-link capacitance that offsets the shunt capacitance currents, equalising voltage across discs.
why: Longer cross-arms help (lower shunt capacitance), shorter ones hurt.
Shunt capacitance is the cause of unequal distribution.

q: Base impedance in a per-unit system is given by:
explanation: Z_{base} = V_{base}^{2}/S_{base}; with kV and MVA the result is in ohms.

q: Base impedance for 132 kV and 100 MVA base is about:
why: Equals 132/√3, a phase voltage, not an impedance.

q: A generator has X = 0.2 p.u. on its own rating of 50 MVA, 11 kV. Its reactance on a 100 MVA, 11 kV base is:
why: Ignores the change of MVA base.

q: An advantage of the per-unit system is that:
options: It removes the need for a base
Transformer impedances in p.u. are the same referred to either side
explanation: With bases chosen in the ratio of transformer voltages, p.u. impedance does not depend on the side; values of similar machines fall in narrow ranges.

q: Load factor is defined as:
options: Sum of individual maximum demands / maximum demand of the group
explanation: Load factor = average demand ÷ maximum demand over a period (always ≤ 1). Higher load factor means better plant utilisation and lower cost per kWh.

q: Diversity factor is:
options: Always greater than or equal to 1
explanation: Diversity factor = sum of individual maximum demands / maximum demand of the whole system ≥ 1, because consumers do not peak simultaneously.
why: Demand factor is ≤ 1, not diversity factor.

q: Demand factor is defined as:
explanation: Demand factor = maximum demand ÷ connected load; usually less than 1.

q: A consumer uses 876,000 kWh in a year with a maximum demand of 200 kW. Annual load factor is:
why: 50% higher than the correct result — does not follow from the correct working.
2 times too small — a typical formula slip.

q: A 100 MW plant generates 438 GWh in a year. Plant capacity factor is:
why: 2 times too small — a typical formula slip.
Uses GWh directly as a percentage.
20% higher than the correct result — does not follow from the correct working.

q: Four consumers have maximum demands of 20, 30, 25 and 25 kW. The group maximum demand is 80 kW. Diversity factor is:
why: 60% higher than the correct result — does not follow from the correct working.

q: For the same power, power factor and line losses (%), the weight of conductor material required varies with transmission voltage V as:
explanation: I ∝ 1/V; for the same % loss, R must scale as V^{2}, so area ∝ 1/V^{2}: higher transmission voltage saves conductor.

q: If transmission voltage is doubled for the same power and power factor (same conductor), line losses become:
why: Losses depend on I², not I.

q: A 3-phase line delivers 10 MW at 132 kV, 0.9 pf. Each conductor has 5 Ω resistance. Total line loss is about:
A transmission line up to about 80 km length is classified as a:
explanation: Short (< ~80 km): capacitance neglected. Medium (~80–250 km): nominal-T or π. Long (> ~250 km): distributed parameters.

q: Transposition of overhead line conductors is done to:
options: Balance the inductance and capacitance of the three phases
explanation: Each conductor occupies each position for one-third of the length, making the phase impedances equal and reducing interference with nearby communication lines.
why: Corona depends on diameter and spacing.
Sag depends on tension and weight.

q: Inductance of a line decreases when:
explanation: L = 2×10^{-7} ln(D/r′) H/m: larger radius (r′ = 0.7788r) lowers L; larger spacing D raises it.
why: Inductance does not depend on frequency (reactance does).

q: A line conductor weighs 6 N/m, span 200 m, tension 12 kN, supports at equal level. Sag is:
Power available from a hydro plant is given by P = :
explanation: P = ρ g Q H η watts (Q in m^{3}/s, H in m). In kW: P ≈ 9.81 Q H η.
why: η must multiply, and g is missing.

q: A hydro plant has discharge 100 m^{3}/s, net head 100 m and overall efficiency 90%. Power output is about:
Pelton wheel turbines are used for:
explanation: Pelton is an impulse turbine for high heads (roughly > 250–300 m). Francis (reaction) suits medium heads; Kaplan (propeller) low heads.
why: Bulb/Kaplan units are used in tidal plants.

q: Kaplan turbines are most suitable for:
explanation: Kaplan is an axial-flow reaction turbine with adjustable blades, efficient at low heads and large, variable discharge.
why: Reversible Francis pump-turbines are usual in pumped storage.

q: The purpose of a surge tank in a hydro plant is to:
options: Protect the penstock/tunnel against water hammer
explanation: It absorbs pressure rise when turbine gates close suddenly and supplies water when they open, protecting the conduit.
why: Head is set by geography and dam height.

q: HVDC transmission is preferred over HVAC mainly for:
options: Long-distance bulk power and asynchronous interconnection
explanation: Beyond the break-even distance (~600–800 km overhead, much less for submarine cable) HVDC is cheaper; it has no charging current, no stability limit and links grids of different frequency.
why: Converter costs make HVDC uneconomic for short lines.

q: Which is a disadvantage of HVDC transmission?
options: Costly converter stations and harmonic filters
explanation: Converter transformers, valves and filters are expensive and generate harmonics; DC circuit breaking is also difficult.

q: For an underground cable, the dielectric stress is maximum:
options: At the surface of the conductor
explanation: g = V/(x ln(R/r)) is largest at x = r. Grading (capacitance or intersheath) equalises stress. Most economical core size when ln(R/r) = 1, i.e. R/r = e.
why: Stress falls monotonically from conductor outward.
Only with graded insulation is it more uniform.
Stress is minimum at the sheath.

q: Compared with an overhead line of the same voltage, an underground cable has:
options: Much higher capacitance and charging current
explanation: Conductor-to-sheath spacing is small and permittivity of insulation is high, so capacitance is large; surge impedance is low (~40–60 Ω).

q: In a ring main distribution system:
options: Voltage regulation is always poorer than radial
Each consumer is fed from one end only
Supply can reach consumers from either side, improving reliability
explanation: A fault on one section can be isolated and supply maintained from the other side; voltage fluctuations are also less than in long radial feeders.
why: Regulation is usually better than radial.

q: Kelvin's law is used to find the:
explanation: Most economical conductor area is when annual interest and depreciation on capital cost of conductor equals annual cost of energy lost.
why: Economical pf uses a different method (cost of kVAR vs kVA).

q: In load-flow studies, a generator bus with specified real power and voltage magnitude is called a:
explanation: PV (voltage-controlled) bus: P and |V| specified. PQ (load) bus: P and Q specified. Slack (swing) bus: |V| and δ specified, supplies the losses.
why: PQ bus is a load bus.
Slack bus specifies V and δ.

q: Compared with Gauss–Seidel, the Newton–Raphson load-flow method:
options: Has quadratic convergence and needs fewer iterations
explanation: N–R uses the Jacobian and converges quadratically in 3–5 iterations, almost independent of system size, though each iteration is heavier.
why: The Jacobian is the core of N–R.

q: For a lossless line with V_{s} = V_{r} = 1 p.u. and X = 0.5 p.u., the maximum (steady-state) power transfer is:
Series capacitors are used in long transmission lines primarily to:
options: Increase power transfer capability by reducing net series reactance
explanation: Since P_{max} = V_{s}V_{r}/X, reducing X via series compensation raises transfer and stability limits.

q: A 100 kW load at 0.6 pf lagging is to be improved to 0.9 pf lagging. Required capacitor kVAR is about:
explanation: ≈ 84.9 kVAR
why: That is the original kVAR, not the correction.
18% higher than the correct result — does not follow from the correct working.
Only the final tan φ_{2} × P.

q: For economic load dispatch among thermal units (losses neglected), units should operate at:
explanation: Minimum total cost occurs when dC_{1}/dP_{1} = dC_{2}/dP_{2} = … = λ.

q: In an AC network, reactive power mainly flows:
options: From the bus of higher voltage magnitude to the bus of lower voltage magnitude
From the leading-angle bus to the lagging-angle bus
Not at all in transmission lines
explanation: Q ≈ V(V_{s} − V_{r})/X depends on voltage magnitude difference; real power depends on angle difference.
why: Reactive power can flow both ways.
Lines both generate and absorb reactive power.

q: Equal area criterion is used to determine:
options: Steady-state stability of a multi-machine system
Transient stability of a single machine connected to an infinite bus
explanation: It compares accelerating and decelerating areas on the P–δ curve to find the critical clearing angle for a one-machine infinite-bus system.
why: Multi-machine studies need numerical solution of swing equations.
